summary:
Consensual same-sex relations have been legal in Tajikistan since May 1998, sex between women was never criminalised, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. That legality carries no protective apparatus. No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity: the country's first anti-discrimination statute, adopted in July 2022, dropped both grounds and retains only "sex", and a monitoring review covering 2024 finds it only partially aligned with international standards.

Police maintain a register of LGBTIQ people introduced in 2016, and a separate account dates a government registry of "proven" LGBT persons to 2017. The 2024 review records police luring LGBT people into fake meetings in order to register them in a database, harvesting their social-media contacts and extorting money, with more than ten such cases documented in Sughd province. Raids in 2022 and 2023 brought forced HIV testing and arbitrary criminal charges, and ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by officers are documented.

ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people in Tajikistan during 2024, involving arbitrary police arrest, blackmail and extortion. That is a raw count of recorded cases with no population denominator, so it measures what was reported and recorded rather than per-capita exposure. The 2024 review separately documents forced or sham marriages imposed on LGBT people with police declining to intervene.

For a trans visitor the document environment is restrictive. Tajik law permits gender reassignment on some documents, but medical institutions issue no official documents for that purpose. A diagnosis of transsexualism is required, surgery is required for transgender women but not men, and evaluation is by a commission of three psychiatrists on an unregulated case-by-case basis in which activists say bribes are often necessary. Only three to six people are recorded as having changed legal gender.

Gender-affirming medical services are not available in the country, trans people must go abroad to transition medically, and most doctors have no expertise in the treatments trans people need. LGBTQ patients report disrespectful treatment by medical staff, and some psychologists and doctors offer pseudoscientific "cure methods" that treat homosexuality as an addiction comparable to alcoholism or drug dependence. A trans-focused non-governmental organisation has drafted a hormone-replacement-therapy protocol used to educate endocrinologists.

No relationship-recognition framework exists: same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal protections available to married heterosexual couples, so a trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no recognition to rely on. Public expression of support for LGBTQ people is effectively suppressed and public attitudes have been described as "entirely negative", with homophobic and transphobic remarks from politicians forming part of everyday politics. The Supreme Mufti, Saidmukarram Abdulkodirzoda, has called same-sex relations a "disaster", condemned countries legalising same-sex marriage and spoken against human-rights activists and anti-discrimination laws.

LGBTQ groups operate anonymously, one focused solely on trans issues and one on general LGBTQ issues, and activists have no access to the Ministry of Health or other state authorities, which makes state-level advocacy impossible. A legislative analysis built from questionnaires completed by local partners records barriers and gaps for gay men, men who have sex with men and trans people, including situations where the written law protects but practice does not.

The most recent documented incidents in this record are from 2024; no later instance is recorded. An account from January 2013 describes people who disclose their orientation becoming targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police, and characterises the community as one of the most closed in society.
tangentialFactors:
The legal position sits inside a wider repressive state context. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2017 records that the human-rights situation in Tajikistan deteriorated sharply during 2016, with opposition leadership sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned and a predetermined referendum extending presidential rule; the 2016 police register of LGBTIQ people was introduced in that same period.

Two figures in the record are raw counts and should be read as such. The 27 violation cases logged by ECOM in 2024 and the more than ten police-entrapment cases documented in Sughd province are counts of recorded incidents with no population denominator, and Sughd is one province among several; neither supports a per-capita comparison between provinces or countries.

ECOM's 2024 study on trans people's access to medical services, covering HIV prevention and treatment and hormone replacement therapy across the wider region, was contributed to by a Tajikistan country coordinator and includes guidance for trans migrants. The inventory does not set out its Tajikistan-specific findings.

Residents have no non-discrimination protection on sexual orientation or gender identity under the July 2022 statute, which retains only "sex", and no relationship-recognition framework. outOfScopeNotes:
No information in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules, border or airport screening, document markers on passports, or any outing risk during inspection for Tajikistan. Those questions are unresolved here rather than cleared.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records prison and detention references for Tajikistan concerning opposition figures and deportees; no placement or conditions of trans detainees are recorded, so trans detention conditions remain unsourced.

The inventory contains no findings on LGBTQ minors, education-sector policies or school environments, and nothing on how a marriage or partnership involving a trans person would be treated legally. Whether the 2016 police register and the 2017 government registry are the same instrument, and whether either remains operational, is not sourced.

Several social-climate claims rest on a tertiary encyclopaedia entry rather than a primary monitor, and the January 2013 account of abuse after disclosure is more than a decade old; both are carried as dated, attributed material rather than as current prevalence.
